title: Well, which is it? Misinterpretations of the Lawton Principles in the age of nature recovery and artificial intelligence
content:
Misquoted or misrepresented ecological principles are echoed through large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, with implications for study and practice. We present a case study to encourage careful scientific communication and informed use of LLMs for learning.


Abstract

The biodiversity crisis requires responses that are both scientifically sound and socially resonant. Simplified policy messages play a critical role in translating complex ecological goals into concepts that are accessible, actionable and meaningful for diverse stakeholders, helping align local actions with national and international targets. This paper examines the Lawton Review (Making Space for Nature, 2010) as a landmark example of effective policy messaging and reflects on how its core principles have been interpreted and applied over the past 15 years. We analyse the original intent of the Lawton Review's principles: ‘More, bigger, better and joined’, and review how these principles are presented and used by a range of organisations across policy, practice and advocacy. Practical implication. While the Lawton principles were designed to simplify and communicate complex ecological theory, we find they are frequently misquoted or misrepresented. Such inconsistencies risk undermining both effective implementation and accurate knowledge transfer. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of simplified policy messages to distortion, with implications for biodiversity action and for knowledge dissemination in an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence and large language models.
